subject: Effect of mean-centering and FIML on estimates and chi-square

messages.author: f9a02a1a390eea1a
messages.subject: Effect of mean-centering and FIML on estimates and chi-square
parts:
Hi,

I am fitting an SEM to simulated data consisting of 10000 observations of 5 observed variables. Each latent factor in the model has a single indicator and the error variance of the indicator is predetermined using the reliability of each observed variable.

My question relates to the relationship between mean centering and accounting for missingness using full-information maximum likelihood. If I ignore missingness, as expected the model fit and model results are identical on both raw data and on mean-centered data (the same data set with each variable centered on zero, using R’s scale(dat, center=T, scale=F)).

However, if some observations are removed from the data set and the same model refitted using missing=”fiml”, then the version without mean-centering yields different standardised loadings, different exogenous latent variances, and a chi-squared statistic of the order of 10000 times larger. Why does mean-centering make such a difference in the case where there is missing data, or is this something to do with the treatment of “fiml” under the hood? I’d really appreciate an explanation of what is going on and what I can do about it!

The model and some output:

mod <-   "    f1 =~ 1*x1                                                 # single indicator loadings fixed at 1

              f2 =~ 1*x2

              f3 =~ 1*x3

              f4 =~ 1*x4

              f5 =~ 1*x5

 

              f2 ~ f1                                                                # structural model

              f3 ~ f1 + f2

              f4 ~ f3

              f5 ~ f4

 

              x1 ~~ 4.01*x1                                                  # error variances fixed at (1-r)*var(x)

              x2 ~~ 0.23*x2

              x3 ~~ 9.41*x3

              x4 ~~ 0.09*x4

              x5 ~~ 37.65*x5    "

 

Fitted using:

fit1 <- lavaan(mod, data=dat, verbose=T, estimator="MLR", std.lv=F, auto.fix.first=F, orthogonal.y=T, auto.fix.single=F, auto.var=T, auto.cov.lv.x=T, auto.cov.y=F, likelihood="wishart", model.type="sem", missing="ml")

fit2 <- lavaan(mod, data=dat_centered, verbose=T, estimator="MLR", std.lv=F, auto.fix.first=F, orthogonal.y=T, auto.fix.single=F, auto.var=T, auto.cov.lv.x=T, auto.cov.y=F, likelihood="wishart", model.type="sem", missing="ml")

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Effect of mean-centering and FIML on estimates and chi-square
parts: If I ignore missingness, as expected the model fit and model results are identical on both raw data and on mean-centered data

What does "ignore" mean?  If you are using the default (listwise deletion), this is not generally true (but might coincidentally be in your data), unless you centered around the mean of the complete-case data.
However, if some observations are removed from the data set and the same model refitted using missing=”fiml”,

What observations did you remove?  Obviously not cases with missing values, if you are still using FIML.  My comment above might be relevant here, if you just drew a random subsample of data.  It should also depend on whether the variables were centered around the full-sample means or subsample means.

Pat's point is important: make sure you actually estimate the intercepts even if you centered variables.  If the mean structure is saturated, there is no point mean centering anyway.

Finally, the FIML approach will use all available data to estimate the parameters.  Complex missing-data patterns make it difficult to guess from mere sample stats what the ML-estimated mean should be, if you do want to continue mean-centering for some reason.  You could estimate the model with estimated intercepts (e.g., set int.ov.free or int.lv.free=TRUE, the former is the default in sem(), see ?lavOptions for details) using FIML, then extract the saturated-model estimated means using lavInspect(fit, "sampstat").

Some of these issues are discussed in Savalei & Yuan's (2009) article on the model-based ("Bollen-Stine") bootstrap with missing data, if you are interested:  http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/00273170903333590

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
